USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture and engage in resumed negotiations without making new commitments. The US occupies a position of relative leverage — China's economy is slowing to a 27-year low (6.2% Q2 GDP, reported July 15), our Huawei Entity List action has exposed a critical dependency ($11B+ in annual US component sales to Huawei), and the G20 Osaka truce has reopened talks without requiring us to roll back any existing tariffs. However, escalating further risks burning through that leverage by triggering consumer pain on the remaining ~$300B in untariffed Chinese imports (electronics, phones, clothing) and handing China a justification for retaliatory rare-earth restrictions. The smart play is to hold what we have and negotiate.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of -0.2 reflects a mild US advantage. China is under considerably more pressure: Q2 growth hit a 27-year low (NYT, July 15), exports fell 1.3% in June, tariffed exports to the US dropped 30% on the $50B list (Capital Economics, June 25), and industrial production and private investment are weakening. By contrast, the US economy, while showing signs of drag — Atlanta Fed estimating Q2 at just 1.3%, OECD warning that full escalation could cut 0.8% from US GDP — is still fundamentally sound with unemployment low and consumer spending intact. The Huawei Entity List placement (May 16) is a powerful lever: US chip suppliers like Qualcomm, Micron, and Qorvo took immediate stock hits, but this also demonstrates that Huawei cannot replace US technology in the near term (CNBC, May 17). Trump's G20 signal about easing Huawei restrictions (June 29) without actually removing them from the Entity List preserves this as a bargaining chip. China's rare-earth threat (Xi's Jiangxi visit May 20, NDRC statements) is more bark than bite — China lost a WTO case on rare-earth export quotas in 2015, and cutting off supply would damage China's own credibility as a manufacturing hub and hurt Japan/Korea allies who would then pivot harder away from Chinese dependency (NYT, May 23). The action score of 0.0 (hold) is justified because: (1) the G20 Osaka agreement has already restarted talks — no reason to preemptively escalate or concede; (2) the threat of List 4 tariffs on the remaining ~$300B gives us leverage in negotiations, but actually implementing it would hit iPhones, laptops, and consumer electronics directly, generating visible domestic political backlash ahead of 2020; (3) the Temporary General License for Huawei expires Aug 19, giving us a natural pressure point without needing new actions. The OECD estimates current tariffs are already a modest drag on US GDP (0.2-0.3% by 2021-22) and raising consumer prices by 0.3%. Further escalation would compound these costs asymmetrically on US consumers while China has already absorbed the worst of the export shock. Patience and negotiation serve US interests better than either escalation or concession at this juncture.
key_factors: China Q2 GDP at 27-year low (6.2%) — trade war biting harder on Beijing than Washington
Huawei Entity List placement ($11B+ US supplier revenue at stake) gives significant leverage
G20 Osaka truce reopened talks without US concessions — favorable position
List 4 tariffs on ~$300B remaining imports would hit consumer electronics directly — political risk
Rare earth threat from China is limited by WTO precedent and supply chain complexity
OECD warns full escalation could cut 0.8% US GDP — escalation has real costs
US Q2 GDP estimated at only 1.3% by Atlanta Fed — economy slowing but not in crisis
Consumer prices already rising $767/family from existing tariffs (Trade Partnership estimate)

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump tweets that negotiations are going 'too slowly' and that China is attempting to 'renegotiate.' Orders List 3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10 and directs preparation of tariffs on remaining Chinese imports (~$300B).
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.

Google suspends Huawei's access to Android updates / GMS; major US chip suppliers pause sales. Same day: Xi Jinping visits a rare-earth facility in Jiangxi (widely read as a signal on rare-earth leverage).
G20 Osaka: Trump and Xi agree to resume talks. Existing tariffs remain; no new tariffs 'for the time being.' Trump says he will ease some Huawei restrictions (Huawei remains on the Entity List).

China's growth fell to its slowest pace in nearly 30 years — 6.2% in Q2, down from 6.4%. Trade talks broke down on May 10 and President Trump raised tariffs sharply, damaging consumer confidence within China.
Shares of Huawei's key U.S.-listed suppliers including Qualcomm and Qorvo stumbled. Huawei spends $1 out of every $7 of its $70 billion procurement budget on US components.

The currently implemented tariffs are expected to reduce the level of real GDP in China by 0.25 percent and US GDP by 0.19 percent. If US hikes tariffs on remainder of Chinese goods, Chinese GDP would fall by 0.39% and US by 0.31%.
China supplied 80% of the rare earths imported by the United States from 2014 to 2017. It would take years to build enough processing plants to match China's processing capacity.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain current posture. Hold retaliatory tariffs as leverage but do not escalate further. Use the G20 Osaka truce window to pursue structured negotiations while accelerating domestic tech self-sufficiency and supply-chain diversification. Do not offer structural concessions prematurely — the US has demonstrated it will escalate regardless of China's concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.45 reflects a serious but not yet existential situation. On the tariff front, the US has imposed 25% duties on ~$250B of Chinese goods (timeline: List 3 raised May 10), and China has retaliated on ~$60B. China's Q2 GDP fell to 6.2% (NYT, July 15) — a 27-year low but still within the government's 6-6.5% target band. The IMF (June 5) says current stimulus is 'sufficient to stabilize growth 2019/20' absent further tariff hikes. Imports from the US plunged 31% in June (NBC, July 12), but China's retaliatory list is smaller and running out of room — China has ~$60B in retaliatory coverage vs. US coverage of ~$250B, an asymmetric exposure.

The Huawei Entity List action (May 16) represents the most dangerous escalation — it directly threatens China's tech sector and the Made in China 2025 agenda. Huawei relies on US chips for about one-third of its supply chain (PBS, May 29). Google suspended Android access (May 20). This is a structural chokepoint, not just a trade dispute. However, the G20 Osaka truce (June 29) provides a pause: no new tariffs 'for the time being,' and Trump indicated willingness to ease some Huawei restrictions. Supply chains are already shifting to GSP countries, but the scale remains small ($750M in Q1, per Maritime Executive).

On action: the hold recommendation (-0.1) reflects the fragility of the current moment. China should not escalate — the economy cannot absorb further tariff damage, and the Huawei situation requires careful management. But China should not concede either: Trump has shown a pattern of escalating after receiving concessions (renegotiating after the May talks broke down, per timeline May 5), and structural IP/tech-transfer demands in a deal would constrain China's development trajectory. The right move is to negotiate from the current position while building long-term resilience through tech self-sufficiency and rare-earth leverage (Xi's Jiangxi visit, May 20). Conceding purchases alone without structural reform on enforcement mechanisms would lock in an unfavorable dynamic.
key_factors: Q2 GDP at 6.2% — 27-year low but within target; stimulus sufficient per IMF
Huawei Entity List (May 16) strikes at tech ambitions — structural threat beyond tariffs
Asymmetric tariff exposure: US covers ~$250B vs China's ~$60B retaliation capacity
G20 Osaka truce (June 29) provides fragile negotiation window
Supply chain shift to GSP countries underway but still small scale
Xi rare-earth facility visit (May 20) signals untapped retaliatory leverage
Trump pattern of escalating after concessions argues against premature concession
